candidates.title: Scalable and Adaptive Log-based Anomaly Detection: A Synergistic Approach
candidates.abstract: System logs are critical for software reliability. While many automated log-based anomaly detection methods exist, they often falter in large-scale cloud systems due to high resource consumption and poor adaptability to evolving logs. In this paper, we present SeaLog, an accurate, lightweight, and adaptive log-based anomaly detection framework that synergistically integrates the efficiency of traditional data-driven methods with the zero/few-shot learning ability of large language models (LLMs). SeaLog consists of a lightweight detection agent and a backbone analyzer. The detection agent utilizes an n-gram probabilistic tree (NPT) for efficient anomaly detection. The backbone analyzer employs an LLM enhanced by in-context learning (ICL) to provide accurate and adaptive predictions, especially for unseen log data. Both components continuously benefit from anomalies confirmed by on-site engineers. We evaluate SeaLog on three public datasets (BGL, Thunderbird, and HDFS) and an industrial dataset, with multiple LLM backbones, including open-source models, to assess its robustness to model choice. SeaLog achieves strong effectiveness across all datasets (F1 scores of 0.949–0.999), runs 2× to 5× faster, and consumes only 5% to 41% of the memory resources. Furthermore, we have successfully deployed SeaLog in Huawei Cloud, from which we share our insights and experiences during this deployment.

candidates.title: GALLog: A Graph-based Log Anomaly Detection Method with Active Learning
candidates.abstract: System logs continuously record the status and internal operation details of the system, playing a vital role in locating and resolving software anomalies. Recently, numerous deep learning-based methods have been proposed to detect system anomalies via log analysis. However, there are still several critical challenges remain to be addressed. First, existing methods are highly dependent on expensive and manually-curated labeling information. Second, the mainstream method of using sequence models to represent log information can be insufficient. To tackle these challenges, we propose GALLog, a graph-based log anomaly detection method that incorporates active learning. GALLog starts by transforming log sequences into graphs and learns neglected structural information in sequence models by graph attention network. To maximize the use of limited labeling budget, we introduce a hybrid active learning strategy to select valuable log entries for labeling. Specifically, the representative strategy ensures samples diversity while the uncertainty strategy focuses on capturing low-confidence samples. Additionally, we designed a data augmentation method using graph representation learning, which is used to reduce sample redundancy and further enhance uncertain samples. Experiments indicate that GALLog outperforms compared approaches under realistic low labeling budgets, and extensive ablation experiments have proven the effectiveness of each component in our design.

candidates.title: Multi-modal artificial intelligence-driven code quality prediction and self-healing automation using self-modulating convolutional neural networks
candidates.abstract: Ensuring software code quality and reliability in contemporary large-scale systems is an important problem with the soaring complexity of software architecture, varied data modalities, and adaptive execution environments. This research proposes a Multi-Modal Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Driven Code Quality Prediction (CQP) and Self-Healing Automation framework using a Self-Modulating Convolutional Neural Network framework (CQP-SHA-SMCNN). The framework starts with a data gathering stage that combines diverse modalities of software artifacts such as source code repositories, static analysis reports, run logs, and developer comments. These heterogeneous sources are transformed into homogeneous feature spaces using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) based feature extraction to represent the structural, semantic, and behavioral characteristics of the code. The Self-Healing Automation (SHA) Pipeline observes software systems, forecasting imminent quality degradations and runtime. In case a fault is detected, the pipeline applies the Self-Modulating Convolutional Neural Network (SMCNN) model to perform root-cause analysis and triggers self-healing, such as code patch proposals, automatic refactoring, or runtime reinit. This research proposes a Multi-Modal Artificial Intelligence-driven framework for software code quality prediction and self-healing automation, in which the implemented artificial intelligence technique is a Self-Modulating Convolutional Neural Network applied to automated software quality assessment, fault diagnosis, and self-healing maintenance. Performance is evaluated using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves, Precision, Recall, F-measure (F1-score), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and compared with existing methods. The study demonstrates the potential of AI-driven Deep Learning (DL) models for automated software quality prediction and intelligent self-healing maintenance in modern environments.

candidates.title: Modeling and analysis of teacher-student interaction in electronic commerce courses from a multidimensional interaction perspective
candidates.abstract: Teaching activities in e-commerce courses are increasingly supported by digital platforms and multimodal data records. Teacher–student interaction behavior is therefore characterized by high-dimensional, heterogeneous, and dynamically changing evidence, which provides a data basis for fine-grained classroom interaction analysis. This study proposes a multidimensional framework for modeling teacher–student interaction behavior by integrating temporal analysis and graph-based relationship representation across four heterogeneous data sources: video, audio, operation logs, and discussion texts. It uses timestamp alignment, window segmentation, and semantic coding to construct a four-dimensional feature matrix comprising visual, auditory, operational, and semantic dimensions. The model was evaluated on a dataset containing 120 class sessions from five e-commerce courses. The proposed model achieved an accuracy of 91.3%, a Macro-F1 score of 90.1%, an AUC of 95.2%, a sequence consistency score of 88.9%, and an anomaly detection recall of 86.7%. Compared with the single-mode CNN-LSTM baseline, the accuracy increased from 87.4 to 91.3%, corresponding to an improvement of 3.9 percentage points. Compared with the Graph Transformer baseline, the proposed model improved accuracy by 0.6 percentage points and anomaly detection recall by 0.9 percentage points. In real-world teaching scenarios, the model achieved an average system response latency of 41.2 ± 3.5 ms, an interaction chain complete recognition rate of 91.1 ± 2.2%, an anomaly segment localization accuracy of 88.1 ± 2.4%, a teacher feedback trigger effectiveness of 86.2 ± 2.5%, and a classroom conversation coverage of 93.7 ± 1.8%. These results indicate that multimodal fusion, teacher–student bipartite interaction graph constraints, and temporal dependency modeling jointly improve interaction recognition and abnormal segment detection. However, the relatively weaker performance in promotional campaign planning shows that the current 32-window sequence and teacher–student bipartite graph are less effective in open-ended discussions involving delayed responses, parallel peer interactions, and rapid topic transitions. Cross-course transfer therefore remains to be validated across different task structures, semesters, and institutions.

candidates.title: Lessons from the Minab tragedy: protecting education in the age of AI-assisted warfare
candidates.abstract: "The destruction of the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, on February 28, 2026, should force the international community to confront a painful truth: even the most technologically advanced militaries remain capable of catastrophic errors when civilians are insufficiently protected. This article aims to elaborate on lessons learned from Minab and similar tragedies, hoping that although the scientific community cannot by itself prevent wars, it can influence how evidence is gathered; technologies are developed; and accountability is pursued." On February 28, 2026, what began as an ordinary school day at Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School ended in unimaginable tragedy when United States and Israeli missiles "according to multiple public reports and ongoing investigations", struck the school grounds, causing the collapse of large sections of the building and trapping hundreds of children, teachers, and staff beneath the rubble. According to multiple independent investigations, at least 168 people were killed, many of them young students between the ages of seven and twelve [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].The school, known for serving children from the local community, was filled with students attending classes when the attack occurred. Witnesses described scenes of panic as explosions shook the area. Teachers reportedly rushed to protect their pupils, guiding them toward safer parts of the building and attempting to contact parents. Moments later, additional strikes reportedly hit the vicinity, turning the school into a scene of destruction and chaos. Rescue workers, emergency personnel, and local residents immediately began searching through the debris. Images and videos from the aftermath showed shattered classrooms, torn schoolbooks, children's backpacks, and desperate efforts to locate survivors. Families gathered outside the ruins, hoping for news of their children, while hospitals struggled to cope with the large number of casualties and injuries. Due to the distasteful and offensive real images of this catastrophe, an AI generated picture of Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school before and after bombardment is shown in Figure 1 to virtually describe the level of crime and destruction.Figure 1. AI generated by ChatGPT [9].The tragedy sparked widespread grief across Iran and drew international attention. Human-rights organizations condemned the loss of civilian life and called for independent investigations into the circumstances of the attack. Several groups argued that schools are protected civilian sites under international humanitarian law and that all parties to a conflict must take every possible precaution to prevent harm to children. For the people of Minab, the attack left scars that extend far beyond the physical destruction of a school building. Classrooms that once echoed with laughter and learning became symbols of loss. Parents mourned children whose futures were cut short, classmates grieved friends they would never see again, and an entire community struggled to come to terms with the scale of the devastation.The Minab school tragedy stands as a painful reminder of the human cost of armed conflict. Regardless of political disputes and military objectives, the deaths of so many children underscore the profound consequences that war can have on civilians. As investigations and debates continue, the memory of the students, teachers, and families affected by the attack remains a powerful call for accountability, protection of civilians, and the pursuit of peace.The reported destruction of a school in Minab, Iran, and the deaths of large numbers of children have drawn international attention to the vulnerability of educational institutions in conflict zones. While investigations and public accounts continue to examine the circumstances of the incident and questions of responsibility, the event highlights a broader and well-documented concern: the devastating impact of armed conflict on children and their access to education. Schools serve not only as centers of learning but also as places of safety, social development, and community cohesion. When educational facilities are damaged or destroyed during military operations, the consequences extend far beyond the immediate casualties. Survivors often experience long-term psychological trauma, interrupted education, displacement, and reduced access to essential social services. International humanitarian law provides special protections for civilians and civilian infrastructure, including schools. Numerous international organizations have documented the increasing risks faced by children in conflict-affected regions and have called for stronger measures to prevent attacks on educational facilities. Such incidents raise urgent questions regarding civilian protection, accountability, and compliance with established legal norms [1,3].The reported Minab tragedy certainly illustrates how a single event can affect an entire generation [7-8]. Families, friends, educators, healthcare workers, and local communities bear the burden of recovery long after media attention fades. Figure 2 is a painting by an Iranian artists drawn in memory of the innocent children who have lost their life in this tragedy [10]. Beyond the immediate loss of life, the destruction of educational environments can undermine social stability and hinder long-term development. For researchers, policymakers, and humanitarian organizations, incidents involving schools underscore the importance of systematic data collection, independent investigation, and evidence-based policy responses. Understanding the factors that place children at risk during armed conflict is vital for developing effective prevention strategies and strengthening international mechanisms for civilian protection.of political perspectives, the protection of children and educational institutions remains a universal humanitarian imperative. Continued research, transparent investigations, and global cooperation are necessary to reduce the chance of similar tragedies and ensure that schools remain places of learning rather than casualties of war. The tragedy is not simply a story about one school. It is a warning about the growing gap between the sophistication of modern weapons and the reliability of the information systems that guide them. Military planners increasingly rely on vast streams of intelligence data, satellite imagery, automated analysis, and algorithm-assisted decision-making. These technologies promise greater precision and fewer civilian casualties. Nevertheless, the events in Minab demonstrate that precision is meaningful only when the underlying information is accurate and continuously verified. A missile can strike within meters of its intended coordinates and still produce a humanitarian disaster if the coordinates themselves are wrong. Reports surrounding the Minab strike suggest that the school stood near facilities associated with Iran's Revolutionary Guards and that historical information about the area may have influenced targeting assessments. Whether future investigations ultimately attribute the disaster to outdated intelligence, procedural failures, technological shortcomings or human error, the broader lesson remains the same: civilian protection cannot be delegated to assumptions embedded in databases.This challenge extends beyond the Middle East. Around the world, governments are investing heavily in artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and data-driven military planning. Advocates often emphasize speed, efficiency and operational advantage. Far less attention is devoted to the consequences of incorrect data, degraded intelligence or flawed classification systems. When errors occur, they can be amplified by the very technologies designed to improve decision-making. The deaths of children in Minab should therefore be viewed not only as a humanitarian tragedy but also as a policy failure. International law already requires belligerents to distinguish between military objectives and civilian objects and to take all feasible precautions to minimize civilian harm. The question is whether existing accountability mechanisms are keeping pace with rapidly evolving military technologies.The growing integration of artificial intelligence into military decision-support systems raises an additional challenge for International Humanitarian Law. The legal principle of proportionality requires commanders to determine whether the anticipated incidental civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage expected from an attack. This assessment is inherently qualitative, context-dependent, and ultimately a matter of human legal judgment rather than algorithmic optimization. AI systems may assist by processing large volumes of intelligence or identifying potential military objectives, but they cannot independently evaluate the moral, legal, and contextual considerations that proportionality requires. Moreover, AI does not merely provide neutral information. By determining which information is highlighted, how confidence levels are presented, and how rapidly decisions are expected to be made, AI systems actively reshape the conditions under which human judgment is exercised. Automation bias, opaque model behavior, embedded biases in training data, and increasing operational tempo may unintentionally narrow the deliberative space required for careful legal assessment. Ensuring meaningful human control therefore requires more than retaining a human "in the loop"; it requires designing AI-supported decision processes that preserve independent legal judgment, transparency, and accountability.Three reforms deserve urgent consideration. First, countries should adopt stricter independent review procedures for targets located near schools, hospitals, and other protected civilian sites. Second, military investigations involving large-scale civilian casualties should be transparent and subject to external scrutiny. Third, governments developing AI-assisted targeting systems should be required to disclose how such systems are validated, audited, and monitored for error.The children who died in Minab will never benefit from these reforms. However, their deaths should compel policymakers, military leaders and researchers to examine whether current practices are adequate for an era in which a single targeting mistake can extinguish hundreds of futures in a matter of seconds. Scientific and technological progress is often celebrated for expanding human capability. The true measure of that progress, however, is whether it also expands human responsibility. Minab reminds us that the answer remains uncertain. The consequences of attacks on children extend far beyond the immediate death toll. Every classroom contains a reservoir of future human potential that cannot be measured at the moment of loss. Among the students killed in Minab may have been future scientists, physicians, engineers, teachers and innovators whose contributions could have benefited not only their own communities but humanity as a whole.Scientific progress depends on the emergence of talent from diverse social, economic and geographical backgrounds [11]. History repeatedly demonstrates that transformative discoveries often come from unexpected places. The next breakthrough in cancer treatment, renewable energy, climate adaptation, artificial intelligence or public health may originate from a child attending a school far from the world's major research centers. When conflict destroys educational opportunities or claims young lives, society loses not only individuals but also the knowledge, creativity and leadership they might have contributed. The effects are cumulative. Beyond those who perish, surviving classmates may experience trauma, displacement and interruptions to their education. Schools may close, teachers may leave, and families may become reluctant to send children to class. The resulting decline in educational attainment can persist for decades, reducing the number of students who ultimately enter higher education, research and innovation. In this way, a single attack can reverberate through an entire generation. For the global scientific community, the protection of children and educational institutions is therefore not solely a humanitarian concern. It is also an investment in humanity's future intellectual capacity. Every child denied the opportunity to learn represents a possibility lost; every school destroyed narrows the pipeline through which future discoveries emerge. The cost of such violence cannot be calculated only in lives lost today, but also in knowledge, solutions, and progress that the world may never realize.Although the scientific community cannot by itself prevent wars, it can influence how evidence is gathered, how technologies are developed, and how accountability is pursued. For this purpose, several avenues may be proposed as follows:The global research community could support an independent, internationally governed system that documents attacks on schools, universities, hospitals, and other civilian institutions. Using satellite imagery, geospatial analysis, open-source intelligence, and forensic methods, such a network could provide rapid, evidence-based assessments of incidents. Reliable documentation can reduce misinformation, preserve evidence, and support future accountability processes.Scientists, engineers, and legal scholars should collaborate in developing internationally recognized AI assurance frameworks for military decision-support systems. These frameworks should include: auditable workflows documenting how AI contributes to operational decisions; system cards describing intended use, limitations, uncertainty, training data, and known biases; continuous monitoring for concept drift, performance degradation, and changing operational environments; independent verification that AIassisted systems remain compatible with International Humanitarian Law throughout their operational life cycle rather than only during initial deployment.The scientific community has historically shaped norms in areas such as nuclear weapons, biotechnology, and climate science. Similar leadership could help establish norms for AI-assisted warfare.Researchers in geospatial science, remote sensing, and information systems could help maintain verified, continuously updated maps of schools, universities, and other protected civilian sites. If integrated into military planning systems worldwide, such databases could serve as an additional safeguard against accidental targeting.Compared with investment in weapons development, relatively little research funding is devoted to understanding and preventing civilian casualties. Governments, foundations, and academic institutions could support multidisciplinary research involving: conflict studies, artificial intelligence, human rights law, data science, risk assessment, psychology, and trauma recovery. The goal would be to identify systematic ways to reduce harm before military operations occur.Even during periods of geopolitical tension, scientific cooperation often survives when political dialogue breaks down. International scientific organizations such as the International Science Council and agencies within United Nations frameworks can help maintain channels of communication between countries in conflict. Although scientific diplomacy cannot prevent every war, it can create relationships and trust that reduce misunderstandings and encourage de-escalation.The scientific community can advocate for schools and universities to be treated similarly to internationally protected cultural and humanitarian sites. This could include: enhanced monitoring, rapid international investigations after incidents, stronger legal protections, greater political consequences for violations.Prevention is crucial, but so is recovery. Scientists, universities, and funding agencies can provide scholarships, remote learning opportunities, research fellowships, and educational support for children affected by conflict. This helps ensure that the loss of educational opportunity does not become a second tragedy following the initial violence.States developing AI-assisted targeting technologies should ensure that Article 36 reviews under Additional Protocol I extend beyond conventional weapons to encompass the entire AI-enabled decisionsupport process. Because machine-learning systems may evolve after deployment through changing data distributions and operational conditions, legal review should be an ongoing rather than one-time process. Scientists can contribute methodologies for continuous validation, uncertainty estimation, and independent auditing [12][13].Although existing international laws prohibit the targeting of civilian infrastructure, and places such as schools and hospitals, a major problem, particularly in recent years, is that these laws are being flouted openly by governments with little to no consequences. So, while it is important to develop regulations related to the design and use of AI, scientists, engineers, legal scholars, and politicians also need to make sure their governments follow the existing rules. In addition, scientific organizations should collaborate with international bodies investigating attacks on educational institutions by providing technical expertise in digital forensics, satellite imagery, geospatial analysis, and data verification.The scientific community cannot determine where wars are fought, but it can influence how knowledge is used within them. Scientists have helped humanity split the atom, map the genome, and explore distant planets. The same ingenuity should be directed toward a more immediate challenge: ensuring that advances in technology reduce, rather than amplify, the risk to children caught in conflict. Protecting schools is not only a humanitarian obligation; it is a commitment to preserving the minds that will shape humanity's future.

candidates.title: GHA-Agent: A Multi-Agent Framework for GitHub Actions Log Parsing
candidates.abstract: The advent of continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) technologies has significantly reduced development cycles for engineering teams. As the world's largest open-source repository, the GitHub Actions (GHA) platform has rapidly become the preferred tool for developers. However, GHA failures generate massive volumes of unstructured logs, making root cause analysis (RCA) exceptionally challenging. Existing log parsing research primarily focuses on structured system logs, relying on static templates that struggle to handle the highly dynamic and unstructured nature of GHA logs. Although recent explorations into unstructured log parsing have emerged, two core challenges persist in the GHA context: First, there is a lack of a standard benchmark dataset covering the entire process from log parsing to code repair. Second, it is difficult to semantically distinguish among different failure modes such as build errors, test failures, and runtime exceptions. This study proposes a multi-agent log parsing framework and the end-to-end evaluation benchmark GHA-Bench to address these challenges. GHA-Agent is built on an LLM-driven multi-agent architecture for zero-shot error localization in extremely long logs. It integrates autonomous tool invocation with context-aware parsing strategy selection to enable effective reasoning over highly unstructured log data. GHA-Bench includes failure logs from 323 real repositories with manually labeled parsing results and corresponding golden patches, supporting comprehensive evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that GHA-Agent achieves 97.75% error coverage in log parsing. In a downstream manual evaluation, experts accepted the generated log diagnoses for 83.0% of instances and the root-cause reports for 78.0% of instances, indicating that GHA-Agent often preserves evidence useful for code-level diagnosis.

candidates.title: A geometric data augmentation and mechanism modeling framework for class-imbalanced wind turbine fault diagnosis
candidates.abstract: With the growing deployment of wind energy, reliable fault diagnosis of wind turbines (WTs) is increasingly important for sustainable operation and maintenance. However, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system data are often characterized by severe class imbalance and complex correlations among multi-source features, which hinder accurate fault recognition. To address these challenges, this study proposes a geometric visibility augmentation-mechanism supervision graph (GVA-MSG) framework for imbalanced fault diagnosis of WTs. At the data level, GVA integrates visibility-based neighbor filtering, Voronoi-based boundary constraints, and density-adaptive directional filling into the synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) to generate minority samples within class manifolds and alleviate imbalance. At the model level, MSG captures temporal dependencies and introduces mechanism supervision based on the wind speed-power relationship. A mechanistic consistency loss aligns model decisions with physical principles, while a latent-space graph adaptively learns cross-channel feature relationships for fault recognition. Comparative, ablation, and generalization experiments are conducted on real SCADA datasets. GVA-MSG achieves a Macro-Accuracy, Macro-F1, and Macro-Gmean of 98.57 %, 96.42 %, and 97.75 %, respectively. Compared with the best-performing data generation baseline, these metrics improve by 1.29, 3.55, and 2.94 percentage points; compared with the best-performing diagnostic baseline, they improve by 0.17, 0.44, and 0.28 percentage points. These results demonstrate that GVA-MSG improves class balance, the quality of generated samples, and mechanism-supervised feature characterization. Moreover, the cross-wind-farm validation results indicate that GVA-MSG maintains stable performance under the tested distribution shifts, demonstrating promising transfer stability and application potential under the current validation conditions.

candidates.title: Hybrid model for detecting Denial of Wallet attacks in serverless architectures
candidates.abstract: Abstract Serverless architectures enable application execution in environments where computational resources are allocated dynamically. Unlike traditional models, functions are invoked based on discrete events, offering scalability and reduced operational overhead. However, the ephemeral and distributed nature of these environments introduces significant monitoring challenges, rendering them vulnerable to exploitation. A Denial of Wallet (DoW) attack represents a specific threat in cloud-native ecosystems, where an attacker deliberately exhausts a target’s financial resources by forcing consumption beyond budget thresholds. Such attacks exploit the pay-per-use billing model, leading to substantial financial liabilities. This study introduces a hybrid detection model for DoW attacks that combines traditional statistical methods with advanced AI techniques to reduce computational costs while maintaining detection efficacy. The proposed framework operates in two sequential phases. First, time-series entropy is derived from the distribution of function invocation types and execution-duration buckets, generating a temporal sequence reflecting system behavior. Second, a supervised anomaly detection algorithm is applied to this sequence to identify deviations indicative of a DoW attack. This entropy-driven approach aims to enhance accuracy while minimizing false positives. By quantifying the randomness and predictability of serverless workloads, the model provides an effective mechanism for early threat identification, enabling proactive identification of financial risks associated with Denial of Wallet attacks in offline and batch evaluation settings. This dual-phase strategy ensures the effectiveness of previously developed methods while significantly improving computational efficiency in serverless deployments.

candidates.title: LLM-Driven Alert Correlation and Lifecycle Prediction With Threat Intelligence for Attack Forensics
candidates.abstract: Security Operations Centers face overwhelming volumes of alerts from firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and other sources. These alerts often lack temporal and semantic coherence, hindering analysts from reconstructing full MITRE ATT&CK lifecycles or anticipating subsequent techniques. To address this, we propose a framework for alert correlation and lifecycle prediction, named LANCE (Lifecycle Analysis with Neural Correlation Engine). LANCE leverages large language models (LLMs) to consolidate heterogeneous alerts into structured, time-ordered sequences, while Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) provides semantic grounding. A Gemma 3-4B LLM serves as the backbone, with lightweight parameter adaptation enabling specialization for cybersecurity tasks without sacrificing real-time efficiency. The design combines three elements: structured prompts that transform raw alerts into coherent narratives, CTI-guided supervision that aligns telemetry with ATT&CK techniques, and efficient adaptation strategies that minimize computational overhead. Results show that without CTI, the highest achievable accuracy is only 27.82%, while integrating CTI improves performance to 64.76%. Using all available telemetry yields the highest prediction accuracy, whereas removing even one source, such as firewall logs, drops accuracy by nearly 30%. Together, these findings show that CTI integration, comprehensive telemetry, and efficient LLM reasoning enable accurate, real-time forensic analysis and proactive defense.

candidates.title: Fault Localization Using LLMs With Line-by-Line Program Execution Traces
candidates.abstract: Fault localization (FL) is a fundamental process for identifying the root causes of software bugs. Although existing methods demonstrate that integrating static code with dynamic runtime information improves accuracy, a limitation remains. Although omniscient debugging tools provide fine-grained, line-level execution traces, their effectiveness in automated fault analysis remains unclear because they are primarily used for manual navigation. In this study, we addressed this limitation by incorporating line-level execution traces into a large language model (LLM)-based FL. We evaluated the approach using 95 single-line, single-method Java bugs selected from Defects4J v1.2 and three LLMs, assuming that the buggy method was known, and compared three input conditions: no trace, stack trace, and line-level execution trace. The execution-trace condition achieved the highest mean reciprocal rank (MRR) for all models, and relative to the no-trace condition, the correct-line ranking improved by 26%–35% for the bugs. The analysis of the improved and degraded cases showed that trace-specific runtime facts were often referenced as evidence in the improved cases, whereas incomplete or mismatched trace information was observed in the degraded cases. In a supplementary analysis of 15 model–bug pairs (30 explanations), explanations with execution traces were more consistently grounded in the provided information and less reliant on speculative reasoning than those without execution traces. For the 10 selected bugs, the median total additional time associated with the execution traces was 8.4 s. These findings indicate that, within the evaluated setting, line-level execution traces can be a useful information source for LLM-based FL.

candidates.title: Confidence-Guided Cross-Modal Knowledge Transfer for Multimodal Anomaly Detection in Microservice Systems
candidates.abstract: Accurate anomaly detection is essential for reliable and secure operations of microservice systems. While an increasing number of studies have shifted from unimodal modeling to multimodal interaction and fusion, effectively leveraging reliable cross-modal information remains challenging. The challenge primarily stems from two aspects. Firstly, different modalities are influenced by factors like load fluctuations, leading to dynamically changing reliability. Secondly, multimodal data exhibit heterogeneity in both structure and semantics. Therefore, we propose a confidence-guided Cross-Modal knowledge Transfer method for multimodal Anomaly Detection (CMT-AD). It jointly models metrics and logs within a unified deep clustering framework and estimates modality reliability through the soft clustering distributions, where clustering uncertainty is quantified into confidence scores. Guided by these confidence scores, the model actively analyzes the contributions of each modality in cross-modal interactions and supplements low-confidence modalities with knowledge from high-confidence ones. To further mitigate cross-modal heterogeneity, we introduce a gated intermediate modality and design structural and semantic consistency constraints that align the original modalities with the intermediate modality to preserve similarity structures and semantic distributions across modalities. Furthermore, intra-modal and cross-modal regularization terms are incorporated to enhance cluster compactness and mitigate negative transfer. We evaluated CMT-AD on three large-scale datasets, and the results demonstrate that CMT-AD outperforms state-of-the-art approaches and achieves an F1-score higher than 0.9.

candidates.title: Absolute Urban Floodwater–Level Estimation from CCTV Imagery via Laser-Scanning–Based Image Projection
candidates.abstract: Abstract Absolute estimation of urban floodwater levels from closed-circuit television (CCTV) imagery remains a challenge, particularly under nighttime illumination, reflections, and rain-induced noise, where segmentation-based and reference-object methods often degrade in performance. Although laser-scanning point clouds provide reliable 3D geometry, their integration with fixed urban CCTV streams for real-time, metric-scale flood monitoring remains insufficiently explored. This study presents a unified CCTV–laser-scanning framework for detecting flood events and estimating absolute floodwater levels in urban environments by integrating a time window–based incident detection scheme with an edge-based adaptive moving-window waterline tracking method. A two-stage photogrammetric calibration procedure—direct linear transformation (DLT) followed by single photo resection (SPR)—recovers camera orientation parameters for uncalibrated CCTV cameras, which enables the generation of image-projected point cloud data from terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) and mobile mapping system (MMS) measurements. Pixel-level water–structure contact lines extracted from CCTV imagery are subsequently projected onto the image-projected point cloud data, enabling metric-scale floodwater-level estimation. The proposed framework was validated under severe nighttime rainfall conditions using four urban CCTV data sets recorded during Typhoon Mitag (2019) in Uljin, South Korea. The results demonstrate reliable flood event detection and accurate floodwater-level estimation, with the latter achieving subdecimeter-level accuracy for both TLS- and MMS-derived point cloud data. These findings indicate that the photogrammetric integration of CCTV imagery with laser scanning offers a practical basis for real-time urban flood monitoring and disaster-response applications.

Causal Root Cause Analysis in Software-Defined Systems: A Review With Context-Aware Causal Observability as a Case Study
candidates.abstract: Software-defined systems, spanning software-defined networking (SDN), software-defined storage (SDS), cyber-physical systems (CPS), IoT, and, more recently, software-defined vehicles (SDVs), are becoming increasingly complex and software-intensive, making reliable diagnosis critical to system performance and, in safety-critical domains, operational safety. Yet formal causal root cause analysis (RCA) methods remain unevenly adopted across these domains, particularly in the emerging SDV context. This paper presents a systematic, PRISMA-based review of causal RCA methods for software-defined systems, categorizing existing approaches according to their level of causal formalism, ranging from structural causal models to probabilistic graphical models and dependency-based approaches, and assessing their applicability to SDVs. The review shows that many existing observability and diagnostic practices remain predominantly correlation-based, limiting their ability to capture true cause-and-effect relationships in dynamic and highly interdependent environments. It further reveals that SDV-specific research on causal RCA remains at an early stage, with existing approaches relying on dependency-based causal reasoning and no adoption of probabilistic or structural causal modeling. This gap is particularly important given the architectural complexity, dynamic interactions, and safety-critical nature of SDVs. Key challenges, including telemetry heterogeneity, real-time constraints, safety-critical operation, and the need for context-aware causal analysis, are examined using SDVs as a representative case study. Finally, the paper outlines future research directions, including causality-aware observability frameworks, contextual causal analysis, open benchmarking infrastructures, and lightweight real-time causal reasoning, toward more explainable, reliable, and safety-aligned diagnostics for software-defined systems.

candidates.title: Apus enables automated end-to-end analysis and quality control of large-cohort proteomics data
candidates.abstract: Translating large-cohort proteomics data into biomedical insights requires timely, scalable, and reproducible data analysis. Here, we present Apus, an end-to-end solution built on a distributed private cloud architecture that automates the entire data analysis workflow, covering real-time data aggregation, parallelized protein identification, high-throughput quantification, comprehensive quality control (QC), and machine learning-driven bioinformatics analysis. We demonstrate the utility of this workflow on a longitudinal experiment, with automated identification and QC in parallel with data generation, enabling real-time monitoring of experimental stability and proactive alerts for potential issues. In a clinical case study, we reanalyzed a 222-run cohort, quantified 6,844 proteins, and identified candidate biomarkers that showed promising discriminatory performance using integrated machine learning methods. Apus provides an automated, user friendly, and robust solution for critical bottlenecks in large-cohort proteomics.

candidates.title: An Empirical Analysis of LLM Usage in Software Engineering Course Projects
candidates.abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have had a substantial impact on software engineering research and practice, as well as on software engineering education. In Software Engineering (SE) education, prior studies have mainly examined students’ LLM usage through surveys, interviews, or short-term observations, offering limited visibility into their actual development activities. As a result, it remains unclear how students’ perceptions of LLM usage match their actual development practices. To address this gap, we analyze course project data collected over three years from 158 students enrolled in an upper-level SE course, together with students’ experience-sharing presentations, survey responses, and activity logs. We examine LLM integration by jointly analyzing students’ perceived usage and usefulness from surveys and presentations, their actual development activities captured through VS Code activity logs, and their project performance based on evaluation results across different levels of LLM support. By combining these analyses, we connect students’ reported LLM usage with their actual development activities and assess its relation to learning outcomes in SE course projects. Our results show that students utilized LLMs frequently for code-related tasks and generally found them helpful, with frequent usage increasing over the course project while perceptions shifted as project complexity grew. Activity log analysis revealed divergent patterns in LLM usage, reflecting both increasing dependency and deliberate efforts to maintain development independence. Across three years, integrating LLM support did not lead to statistically significant differences in final project achievement as measured by requirement satisfaction, although students with LLM support produced substantially larger software systems and lower-performing teams showed mild benefits, suggesting that LLMs may help reduce the influence of programming proficiency on project outcomes. Our findings highlight both the benefits and tensions of LLM integration in SE course projects and suggest that future SE course designs may incorporate more complex and challenging SE tasks beyond implementation-focused requirements, while also providing explicit education on prompt engineering, supporting students’ code comprehension of rapidly generated LLM-assisted code, and helping students avoid excessive dependency on LLM tools during development.

candidates.title: Anomaly Detection Algorithm for Gas Flaring Investigation: The RXD Performance on Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 Data in Southern Iran
candidates.abstract: Satellite-based techniques are increasingly used to monitor gas flaring (GF) and assess its environmental impacts. This study applies the Reed-Xiaoli Detector (RXD) algorithm to identify GF locations in the Pars Special Economic Energy Zone (PSEEZ) in Iran, one of the world’s largest gas reserves. RXD was first implemented on shortwave infrared (SWIR) images from the OLI sensor on Landsat 8/9, and its performance was then evaluated using MSI data from Sentinel-2A/B. All available cloud-free OLI and MSI SWIR reflectance data from 2016 to 2022 were processed. To improve detection robustness, a new step based on the annual persistence of the RXD metric was introduced, ensuring an optimal balance between sensitivity and accuracy. Ground-truth GF locations from field surveys and very high-resolution satellite imagery were used to assess RXD performance. Results show that RXD, on both OLI and MSI, enhances the identification, mapping and monitoring of gas flaring sites compared with existing satellite GF products using similar spectral bands. The demonstrated reliability of RXD outputs highlights the algorithm as a valuable component of a multi-source GF monitoring framework, supporting decision-making for the sustainable management of industrial activities.

candidates.title: IoT4Cows: A LoRaWAN system for cattle monitoring in extensive grazing with network performance evaluation
candidates.abstract: Extensive livestock farming relies mostly on empirical observation for herd health supervision, often leading to delayed disease detection and reduced reproductive performance. These challenges are particularly pronounced in large grazing areas, where animal dispersion and limited cellular connectivity hinder the adoption of conventional monitoring technologies. This paper presents IoT4Cows, an Internet of Things (IoT) system for continuous cattle monitoring in extensive grazing environments. The solution combines a low-power LoRaWAN collar node, equipped with environmental sensors, an accelerometer, a GNSS receiver and a solar panel, with a cloud platform for storage, visualisation, analytics and alerts. The system was evaluated in a seven-week field campaign, including 22 days of continuous functional operation. The campaign involved three cattle within an 88.54 ha grazing area in the Colombian Orinoquía. More than 130,000 communication records were generated during the campaign. Reception was directly verified over 50.3% of the grazing area using a single gateway, while the longest validated link reached 2.21 km beyond the grazing-area boundary. Measured path loss agreed with the link budget, and the link-quality packet reception ratio (PRR) was 0.89. Temperature readings met the sensor specification, whereas humidity met the specification only after decoder-side correction. Measured battery autonomy without solar charging was 4.2 days, while solar charging was projected to extend autonomy beyond this value. Simulation estimated a capacity of approximately 62 nodes per gateway at the deployed SF8 configuration. These results demonstrate the technical feasibility of the IoT4Cows architecture for cattle monitoring under extensive grazing conditions and provide a basis for further evaluation in larger field deployments.

candidates.title: An intelligent IoT-Based system for real-time electrical anomaly detection and protective relay actuation using machine learning
candidates.abstract: Protecting sensitive electrical equipment used in residential, laboratory, and commercial environments from power anomalies is critical to ensure operational safety and reliability. This paper presents a real-time intelligent monitoring and protection system that combines Internet of Things (IoT) sensing with embedded Machine Learning (ML) for anomaly detection. The system is implemented on the M5StickC (ESP32-based) microcontroller using a custom TinyML model developed with Edge Impulse. Device behavior is classified into normal and off states, while anomalous behavior is detected using an unsupervised clustering-based diagnostic layer. Detected anomalies, including unexpected power surges or fluctuations, trigger automated alerts and can optionally disconnect power via an integrated relay. To ensure robustness, the model was trained and tested on multiple devices with diverse power ratings, simulating a wide range of operating conditions without risking sensitive equipment. Sensor data is securely transmitted to the Arduino IoT Cloud, enabling real-time remote monitoring, control, and historical analytics. Experimental evaluation on three representative loads (a 12 W LED lamp, a 24-port PoE network switch, and a ∼1000 W toaster/heater) and a one-week commercial-building deployment demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed prototype as an initial step towards real-time monitoring and anomaly-aware protection of low- and medium-power electrical devices; validation as a fault-protection solution for mission-critical, medical, or industrial-safety applications is outside the scope of this work.

candidates.title: An AI-driven cybersecurity framework for GSaaS: Threat detection in emerging space ecosystems
candidates.abstract: Ground Station as a Service (GSaaS) is transforming satellite ground-segment operations through cloud-native, shared, and multi-tenant infrastructure, creating cybersecurity requirements that extend beyond conventional intrusion detection. This study proposes an AI-driven cybersecurity framework that integrates behavioural anomaly detection, supervised threat classification, contextual risk assessment, risk-aware edge–cloud processing, and policy-constrained response orchestration. A key contribution is the Analyst-Capacity-Aware False-Alarm Burden (AC-FAB) model, which extends conventional false-positive evaluation by relating generated false alarms to available analyst capacity and distinguishing detector-level false positives from those ultimately requiring human investigation. The framework is evaluated through complementary GSaaS-specific and benchmark experiments. A 100,000-event synthetic GSaaS dataset comprising 1,000 operational episodes is used to evaluate the integrated decision pipeline. Incorporating the autoencoder anomaly score into supervised classification reduces the false-positive rate from 7.61% to 6.98%, while risk-aware routing retains 80.09% of evaluated events for local edge processing. Policy validation across 20,000 generated response plans records no tenant-scope, session-scope, or action allow-list violations. Response orchestration reduces analyst-facing false positives from 1,272 to 530, corresponding to a 58.33% reduction in estimated false-alarm burden. Complementary evaluation on NSL-KDD and UNSW-NB15 demonstrates the effect of reconstruction-error threshold calibration, reducing false-positive rates from 38.68% to 3.61% and from 65.69% to 9.52%, respectively, relative to the 50th-percentile reference configuration. These findings show that GSaaS cybersecurity should be evaluated not only by detection performance, but also by operational risk, processing location, response-policy correctness, tenant isolation, and the human capacity required to investigate alerts.

candidates.title: DeCoR: decoupled multiplex causal ranking for microservice root cause analysis
candidates.abstract: Failures in microservice systems can produce correlated symptoms across services, motivating the study of structural information for root-cause localization alongside anomaly-based approaches. We study service-level localization from multivariate monitoring metrics under known fault-onset and metric-to-service mapping assumptions. Existing temporal and multilayer ranking methods rarely use relation-estimation reliability to control node-level information exchange between contemporaneous and lagged evidence. We propose Decoupled Multiplex Causal Ranking (DeCoR) and its core algorithm, Regime-aware Innovation Causal Estimation with Confidence-aware Multiplex Coupling (RICE-CM). RICE-CM derives both evidence types from a shared dynamics model fitted to the pre-fault normal segment. It aggregates edge confidence scores into node reliability, applies nonuniform diagonal coupling between same-metric replicas, and ranks services through reverse PageRank on a supra-adjacency matrix. We evaluated RICE-CM on a 300-case subset drawn from three RCAEval datasets: Sock Shop 1 (SS1), Sock Shop 2 (SS2), and Online Boutique (OB). With dataset-specific coupling settings selected on the same benchmark cases, it achieved Avg@5 scores of 0.6000, 0.7040, and 0.4864 on SS1, SS2, and OB, respectively. It achieved the highest Avg@5 among the evaluated methods on all three datasets and exceeded RUN on OB by 0.0288, while requiring approximately 1/33 of RUN’s runtime per case. Compared with RICE-only, RICE-CM improved Avg@5 by 0.0640, 0.0704, and 0.0624, respectively. Paired tests supported these gains on SS1 and SS2 after Holm correction, but not on OB. Against fixed-coupling RICE-MX, the gains were 0.0720, 0.0400, and 0.0336, respectively, with a Holm-adjusted p value of 0.0456 on each dataset. Positive observed gains over RICE-only occurred across all 12 dataset-fault-type combinations, whereas the coupling-parameter sweep showed dataset-dependent sensitivity. These results support node-reliability-driven nonuniform coupling over fixed coupling within the evaluated benchmarks and task assumptions.

candidates.title: IoT-enabled, multi-sensor fire detection and deep-learning acoustic recognition of illegal logging for forest protection
candidates.abstract: Forest fires and illegal logging are major drivers of deforestation, biodiversity loss, and climate instability, yet both are difficult to monitor in remote forests that lack communication infrastructure. Existing forest-protection systems address fire or illegal logging separately, and commonly rely on Wi-Fi or other short-range links to relay sensor data. This paper presents a system that addresses both threats within a single sensor node. The constituent technologies which include multi-sensor threshold-based fire detection, convolutional neural network (CNN) acoustic classification, and LoRaWAN communication are individually established; the contribution of this work is their integration into one forest-protection architecture built from low-cost commodity component and its end-to-end demonstration from in-forest sensing to cloud alerting. A multi-sensor node built around an ESP32 microcontroller interfaces temperature, humidity, smoke, carbon dioxide, and infrared flame sensors, and applies conjunctive threshold logic for early fire detection. A MAX9814 acoustic sensor captures environmental audio, which is classified by a convolutional neural network trained on Mel-frequency cepstral coefficient (MFCC) features to distinguish chainsaw and axe-cutting sounds from natural forest sounds. Sensor data is transmitted through an RF98 LoRa transceiver to a Dragino LPS8 gateway registered on The Things Network (TTN) and forwarded via webhook to a cloud dashboard that visualizes readings and issues automated alerts. Experimental results demonstrate clear separation between fire and no-fire conditions under controlled testing, successful end-to-end LoRaWAN transmission, and a CNN classification accuracy of 92% across four acoustic classes, demonstrating the feasibility of an integrated, long-range forest-monitoring node intended for low-cost deployment in forest-deficient regions such as Pakistan.
